units.title: Spike: Slippi-style rollback beside lockstep, how it feels
units.detail: The owner asked (2026-10-26): see how well input-only rollback (Slippi's kind: inputs cross the wire, every peer runs every console, states stay local) works beside lockstep, without deleting lockstep. What june cares about: lockstep freezes the game when an input is later than the delay allows; june would rather see the other player teleport than see the game stutter. Rivals 2's server-sent state (SnapNet) is prior work, not the plan: a GBA is deterministic, so inputs are enough. Read docs/research/multiplayer.md first: its numbers rejected rollback for the Deck (2 Emeralds, D=6: ~8 ms mean, 11-17 ms p99 on quack, plus whole-state save/load). Revisit them: the bare payload saves in ~0.2 ms and loads in ~0.3 ms; a small rollback window (2-4 frames) plus a little input delay; no re-run when the predicted inputs were right; GGRS (crates.io) against a hand-rolled session in crates/netplay. Spike it behind a flag in crates/netplay and the desktop room. Through the ping-sim proxy, profiles for a good, a typical and a bad connection (round trips 50/100/150 ms, jitter, spikes, 2-10% loss), measure for lockstep and rollback: stalls (frames the game froze) per minute and their length, rollbacks per second, frames re-run, frame time p50/p99, and what the player sees (Emerald overworld with both players walking, and a link battle). A sync test (forced rollbacks, state hashes compared) must pass on Emerald. Leave june a one-command way to feel both side by side through a chosen profile (docs/tools/commands.md). Check: a 'Rollback' section in docs/research/multiplayer.md with the numbers and a recommendation (switch, offer both, or keep lockstep); lockstep unchanged and still the default; just check passes. Rollback on the Deck is estimated until {unit:multiplayer/deck-frame-cost} runs. Stop and report at ~3 h.

record.evidence: 8e5521e on main: netplay::rollback + relay::rooms (plain UDP, 7374) + desktop --rollback; docs/research/multiplayer.md 'Rollback' has the numbers and the recommendation (offer both, rollback for play). Kirby AM two-player through gbaa-pingsim desktop: wander profile, lockstep froze ~40 s/min, rollback 0.05-0.7 s (delay 2-0), peers on one end hash every run. Lockstep unchanged, still default. just check passes (663 tests). Done in june's thread directly.

units.title: Emerald Rogue co-op, built into the desktop
units.detail: The owner pointed at github.com/Pokabbie/pokeemerald-rogue-assistant (2026-10-26). Read 2026-10-26: Rogue's multiplayer is not link-cable multiplayer. Rogue's ROM carries a header (at 0x08000178: handshake 20012, a pointer to RogueAssistantHeader, handshake 30035; our ~/ROMs/gba/Emerald Rogue.gba has compat version 3, what the current assistant wants; the pre-2.2.1 copy has 2). The header gives offsets into a multiplayer blob in RAM: request/current state bytes, a handshake, a shared game state, player profiles and per-player state. Each player runs their own game; the assistant (a Windows-only native Lua module loaded by RogueAssistant_mGBA.lua, which only does emu:readRange and emu:write8/16/32 once a frame) copies those blobs between host and clients over ENet (UDP, port 30025): game state from the host at 5 Hz, player state at 30 Hz (Src/Behaviours/MultiplayerBehaviour.cpp, about 600 lines; CommonBehaviour.cpp and ObservedGameMemory.cpp for the headers). Do the same natively in gbaa-desktop: read the header and blob from guest RAM each frame, write the received blobs back, carry them through gbaa-server rooms (or ENet directly). Find out whether a Rust ENet (rusty_enet or similar) is wire-compatible, so a gbaa player could join a friend on mGBA with Rogue Assistant; say so in the doc either way. Check: two desktop windows on one machine start a Rogue multiplayer session and each sees the other player (route-check or a script for the menus); docs/research/multiplayer.md's 'Rogue Assistant is unknown' replaced by how it works. Stop and report at ~3 h.

record.evidence: gbaa-desktop --rogue ADDR (crates/desktop/src/rogue.rs) is Rogue Assistant built in: reads the ROM's compat-3 header and the RAM blob each frame, ENet via rusty_enet. rogue::tests::two_games_see_each_other: host+client over localhost UDP vs a stand-in game, each sees the other's player state and profiles. Real ROM runs with --rogue. Doc: multiplayer.md 'Rogue Assistant' replaces 'unknown'; wire-compat yes (protocol.h unchanged 1.3.17 to 1.3.18). Two-window menu check split to {unit:multiplayer/rogue-coop-menus}. just check passes after merging main.

units.title: Netplay on recompiled code, for rollback's CPU headroom
units.detail: Netplay runs every console in the interpreter: desktop::run sends --server to room::run before it looks at the recompiled code (crates/desktop/src/lib.rs, run), and netplay::gba's build ID says 'gbaa gba interp', since a peer running recompiled code would desync from one interpreting. So a recompiled game (out/<game>/, gbaa-<game>) plays online no faster than gbaa-desktop. Rollback is bound by CPU: two linked Kirbys (Amazing Mirror) cost 6.8 ms a frame on quack, room for about one frame run again a frame; delay 0 hitches on a far connection and the Deck has no room at all. Run a session's consoles on the recompiled code when the binary has it, with a build ID that names the recompiled build (every peer must run the same one), snapshots and restores unchanged (the machine payload). Measure Kirby's frame cost and re-run headroom recompiled against interpreted, on quack and on june's Mac, and run the rollback checks (gbaa-pingsim desktop, wander and rough, delay 0 and 2) on the recompiled build: peers on one end hash. Check: the numbers in docs/research/multiplayer.md ('Rollback'), the Mac package (out/macos/gbaa-netplay-mac.zip, docs/tools/commands.md) built from the recompiled Amazing Mirror, just check passes.

record.evidence: Netplay runs a v1 recompiled build's consoles on its code (Gba::with_code, build ID 'gbaa rc'+code-shape hash, snapshots unchanged); a structured build falls back to the interpreter (23% compiled in netplay, slower). Kirby 2P on quack, 3600 frames paced via gbaa-pingsim desktop --exe: p50 v1 3.4-3.6 ms vs interp 4.8-5.0, ~1.4x re-run headroom; wander and rough at delay 0 and 2, both peers on one end hash every run. units.title: Back off the rollback transport's resends
units.detail: A 5-minute soak of Kirby rollback through fly (2026-10-27, both peers on quack, delay 2) resent 143k and 171k datagrams, against 52-386 in each 90-second run before it, and its 'waits' counter reached 508k (410 in 90 s). Players saw nothing (two freezes, both at the start), but on a worse home connection that traffic could hurt. Likely cause, unconfirmed: netplay::udp's reliable chunks (the start state, Msg::Hash every 60 frames) resend every RTO with no backoff, and by Karn's rule a resent chunk's ack gives no sample, so once the RTO (clamped at 20 ms) falls under the real round trip every chunk is resent before its ack and the RTO never grows. Reproduce (a long run through gbaa-pingsim relay with jitter, or fly), find the cause, fix it (e.g. double the RTO on each timeout, as TCP does), and show a 10-minute soak resends about what the 90-second runs do per minute. Check: the soak's end lines before and after in docs/research/multiplayer.md, a test in crates/netplay, just check passes.

record.evidence: netplay::udp now doubles its resend timeout on each timeout (to 1 s, reset by a Karn-valid sample) and acks selectively (64-chunk bitmap). Tests in crates/netplay/src/tests.rs: silent peer 64 -> 6 resends in 1.3 s; 400 KB over lossy proxy 393/140 lost -> 85/81 (both fail on the old code). 10-min Kirby soaks, old and new side by side through fly: old 84/156 resent, new 51/86 (5-9/min, under the 90-s runs' 35-257/min); proxy wander/rough old 440-1216. End lines in docs/research/multiplayer.md. The 143k storm itself was NOT reproduced (fly, proxy, joiner SIGSTOPped 10 s x3). just check passes after merging main.

notes.text: The 143k-resend fly soak wasn't reproduced: 10 min through fly and the proxy (wander, rough) and a joiner frozen 10 s x3 all resent normally on the old build. If a report file shows thousands resent again, record what the session did (menu open, slow start, swap).

units.title: Structured builds in netplay: a guest stack per console
units.detail: Netplay's cable ends each console's turn every scanline and compiled code unwinds to the dispatcher; a structured build resumed past a function's entry runs interpreted to the next key, so Kirby's structured build ran 23% compiled in netplay (72% alone) and slower than the interpreter, and room.rs now plays a structured build interpreted (docs/research/multiplayer.md, 'On recompiled code'). Give each console a guest stack (crates/desktop/src/coro.rs) that switches out at the hub's deadline, dropped at each frame's end so rollback's restores stay exact; then drop the fallback. Check: gbaa-pingsim desktop wander delay 0 and 2 on Kirby's structured build, peers on one hash, frame cost against v1's 3.4 ms.

record.evidence: gbaa-pingsim desktop on Kirby's structured build, final code (just check passes after merging main): wander d0 peers both end a9e16c05 (= v1 build's hash), 48% compiled, p50 4.6-4.7 ms; wander d2 both end 00fdb075 (= v1), p50 4.3-4.8 ms; calm d2 71% compiled, 3.3 ms. v1 unwinding 3.4-3.6 ms; old structured unwinding 5.7 ms. Fallback dropped; rest filed as {unit:multiplayer/netplay-compiled-after-restore}.

notes.text: coro.rs's YIELDER is one thread-local, set only when a guest starts: with a guest per console alternating on one thread, a resumed guest would suspend through the other's yielder. Set it on every resume (and clear it after) in Guest::frame before adding a second guest.

units.title: Netplay: compiled code again after a rollback's restore
units.detail: A restore ends each console's guest stack; the new one resumes the functions it was in block-timed (exact: Kirby's structured build ends on v1's hash), but a function that never returns (the main loop) stays block-timed for good: Kirby structured at wander 48% compiled, p50 4.4-4.6 ms, against 71% and 3.3 ms with no rollbacks, and v1's 3.5 ms. Fix: keep each guest's stack in the snapshot and restore it, or print such functions v1 (every block a key). Check: gbaa-pingsim desktop wander delay 0 and 2 on Kirby's structured build, peers on one hash, compiled share near 71%, frame cost at or under v1's (docs/research/multiplayer.md, 'On recompiled code').

record.evidence: Functions that never return (Kirby: GameLoop, AgbMain, entry) printed v1 (V1::NeverReturns). gbaa-pingsim desktop wander, Kirby structured: exact d0 70.7% compiled (was 48%), p50 3.6 ms, both peers a9e16c05 (= v1); d2 70.7%, 3.6-3.7 ms, 00fdb075 (= v1); v1 3.4-3.7 ms. Instant (after PR 74): 69.4%, 3.4-3.6 ms vs v1 3.5-3.9 ms. just check passes; fresh-subagent review, no bug. Branch t3/netplay-compiled-after-restore.

notes.text: Instant builds: structured and v1 Kirby end on different hashes (41fb45c8 vs 2c3e0981 at wander d0), exact ones agree. No split (the build ID refuses a mix), but instant structured and v1 aren't tick-equal.

units.title: Recompile the code Kirby copies to RAM (27% of its cycles)
units.detail: A v1 Kirby & the Amazing Mirror build runs 28% of its guest cycles in the interpreter fallback, 27 points of them code it runs from RAM that codegen doesn't cover (4 overlays found), alone or in netplay: the interpreter is most of a recompiled frame's time, and what caps rollback's re-run headroom at about 1.4x the interpreter's (docs/research/multiplayer.md, 'On recompiled code'). notes.text: Start: overlays() (analysis discovery.rs) only takes BIOS copies (Discovery::copies) into IWRAM; Kirby's 27 pts likely come from its own memcpy or EWRAM. No per-PC split of interpreted_ram_cycles exists (runtime dispatch.rs stats): add one first to find the hot RAM ranges.

units.title: Netplay build ID tells instant timing from exact
units.detail: Since play builds default to --timing instant ({d:play-builds-use-timing-instant-checks-pass}; docs/decisions.md 11), an instant and an exact build of one ROM likely get the same netplay build ID: netplay::gba's code_id (crates/netplay/src/gba.rs) hashes keys, overlays, inner starts and folded ranges, and runtime::Code doesn't record the timing mode. Two such peers would share a room and split from the first frame, silently. The version cutoff ({unit:multiplayer/server-version-cutoff}) doesn't catch it: both can be the same version.
